08 / 18
The appeal, in full
Grievances & Appeals Department, [Health Plan]  ·  March 2026  ·  Anonymized example
Re: Appeal of Prior Authorization Denial — Sertraline 150 mg Capsule
To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing to appeal the denial of prior authorization for sertraline 150 mg. The denial cites the plan's "Non-Preferred Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) Step Therapy" criteria and requires that the patient first trial vortioxetine (Trintellix) before sertraline can be approved. I respectfully disagree with this determination for the following reasons.
Vortioxetine Is Not a Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor
The denial criterion is titled "Non-Preferred SSRI Step Therapy," yet the required step medication, vortioxetine, is not an SSRI. The FDA classifies vortioxetine as a serotonin modulator and stimulator, and peer-reviewed pharmacology literature consistently describes it as a "multimodal antidepressant" with activity across multiple receptor subtypes, including 5-HT3, 5-HT7, and 5-HT1D antagonism, 5-HT1B partial agonism, and 5-HT1A agonism, in addition to serotonin transporter inhibition (Chen et al., Clinical Pharmacokinetics, 2018). This is a fundamentally different mechanism of action from sertraline, which acts selectively on the serotonin transporter.
Requiring a trial of a pharmacologically distinct medication from a different drug class as a prerequisite for approving an SSRI is inconsistent with the stated step therapy criteria. Step therapy protocols are designed to ensure that patients trial therapeutically equivalent alternatives, not to require a medication from an entirely different class before the clinically indicated one can be used.
Sertraline Is a Guideline-Recommended First-Line Treatment
Sertraline is one of the most extensively studied antidepressants available and is recommended as a first-line treatment option across multiple clinical guidelines. A 2018 Lancet systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing 21 antidepressant drugs for the acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder identified sertraline as among the most acceptable and tolerable antidepressants (Cipriani et al., The Lancet, 2018). The American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines similarly recommend SSRIs as first-line pharmacotherapy for depressive and anxiety disorders.
Sertraline has an established safety profile spanning decades of clinical use and is widely regarded as a well-tolerated, effective medication for the conditions for which it is indicated.
Clinical Rationale
Based on my clinical evaluation, sertraline is the most appropriate medication for this patient's current presentation. As the treating psychiatrist, I have assessed the available treatment options and determined that sertraline is indicated based on the patient's diagnosis, clinical history, and individual treatment needs. Vortioxetine has a different pharmacological profile and is not something I have determined to be clinically appropriate for this patient.
Delay in Treatment Poses Clinical Risk
Requiring the patient to trial a medication that is not clinically indicated, solely to satisfy a step therapy requirement, delays access to appropriate treatment. In psychiatric care, treatment delays can result in worsening of symptoms, decline in daily functioning, and deterioration of the patient's overall clinical status. This is particularly concerning given that the patient has already been evaluated and a treatment plan has been established.
I am requesting a step therapy exception and approval of sertraline 150 mg for this patient. If you need any additional clinical information or would like to discuss this case further, please reach out and we will arrange a time.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
References: 1. Cipriani A, et al. Comparative efficacy and acceptability of 21 antidepressant drugs for the acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder. Lancet. 2018;391(10128):1357-1366.   2. Chen G, et al. Vortioxetine: Clinical Pharmacokinetics and Drug Interactions. Clin Pharmacokinet. 2018;57(6):673-686.

No. 12 · Is it private?
12 / 18

HIPAA, done right.

HIPAA follows your provider, not your data. When Northwell runs AI on your visit, it's protected.
§
A legal contract sits behind it. Any vendor touching your health information must sign a Business Associate Agreement, covering encryption, audits, and what they may never do with your data.
🔒
Your audio is encrypted, kept for a short window, then auto-deleted. The signed note stays in your chart in Epic.
☹
Consumer ChatGPT is different. The free app has no such contract. That's the line between your doctor's AI and the one on your phone.
✔
You're asked, and you can say no. It's introduced before the visit, you can opt out, and so can your doctor.
Northwell Health®

The honest benefit
It's not magic time savings. It's attention. In one study of ambient scribing, doctors' eye contact rose from about 70% to 77% of the visit, with less after-hours charting and lower burnout.
Eye-contact figures: independent 2026 ambient-scribing study, not a Northwell result

Your data, your call

Flip one switch off.

When you use AI on your own, most apps train on your chats unless you say no. With your health in there, turn it off.
Claude: Settings → Privacy → turn OFF "Help improve Claude."
ChatGPT: Settings → Data controls → "Improve the model for everyone" → Off.
Northwell Health®
When you use it on your own

Privacy, plainly.

Your personal ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity account is not the hospital's protected system. Use it, but know the limits.
⏱
"Off" stops training, not instant deletion. Even with training turned off, your chats may sit on their servers about 30 days for safety, then get deleted.
§
A personal account is not HIPAA-protected. The hospital's AI is covered by law. Your own account runs under consumer terms. Same brand, very different protection.
⚠
No system is breach-proof. These are reputable companies, but bugs happen, and a link you share can be seen by others.
✓
The simple rule. Great for general questions. Never paste your Social Security number, full ID, or anything you would not want kept. Treat it like a company's computer, not your doctor.
Northwell Health®

Read the fine print

Useful. But look closer.

Some health apps are genuinely useful. Just know what they are, and what they want from you.
Lotus
Free AI primary care · sponsor-supported
It's free because sponsors pay. Ask whose interest the advice serves.
A clinician signs off, but it's app-first, not a relationship.
It says it does not sell your data. Read the terms yourself.
Hims & Hers
Telehealth · subscription
It's a subscription, not free.
A lot of it is automated, so you may never really talk to a doctor.
Can you ask questions? Do you know why you're on this dose?
Free or subscription, the question is the same: who is this really serving?
